extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and agents who practice before the USPTO; practitioners and regulators involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to evaluate attorney conduct (neglect, communications, false statements, cooperation with OED) and to determine sanctions, reinstatement, and appeals. Applies to evaluating practitioner fitness to practice before the Patent Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority to regulate practitioner conduct (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress gave the USPTO authority to govern the conduct of attorneys who practice before it, including requiring attorneys to show good moral character and the necessary qualifications; the USPTO may suspend or exclude any attorney shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct, or who does not comply with regulations established under section 2(b)(2)(D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO's authority is plenary (Kroll v. Finnerty). This statutory authority provides the baseline for evaluating practitioner fitness and imposing suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of PTO Code vs. PTO Rules (date-based rule selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of the alleged violation determines whether the PTO Code (37 C.F.R. part 10) or the PTO Rules (37 C.F.R. part 11) apply: conduct prior to May 3, 2013 is governed by Part 10; conduct after that date is governed by Part 11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO Rules (Part 11) replaced Part 10 effective May 3, 2013 and are based on the ABA Model Rules; practitioners' conduct is judged under whichever version of the rules was in effect when the conduct occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Rules derived from ABA Model Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO Rules in Part 11 were based on the American Bar Association’s Model Rules of Professional Conduct and were intended to bring standards of ethical practice before the Office into closer conformity with rules adopted by nearly all States and the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive guidance and alignment with ABA standards inform how Part 11 is applied in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving all alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; a respondent has the burden of proving any affirmative defense it relies on by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is defined as evidence that produces a firm belief or conviction in the truth of the allegations; citations: Foster v. AlliedSignal and Cruzan v. Dir., Mo. Dep’t of Health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'clear and convincing' evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Evidence is clear if it is certain, unambiguous, and plain to the understanding, and it is convincing if it is reasonable and persuasive enough to cause the trier of facts to believe it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted judicial formulations (Foster; Cruzan) explaining that the standard produces a firm belief or conviction without hesitancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect and failure to communicate with clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner duties include timely prosecution of patent applications and informing clients of Office communications; neglect includes failing to respond to Office Actions, Notices to File Corrected Application Papers, or Notices of Allowance, and failing to advise or send copies to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts I, III, V, and VII exemplify how failure to respond to PTO deadlines and failure to notify clients leads to abandonment of applications and supports findings of neglect and lack of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making false statements or misrepresentations (to clients or OED) and failure to cooperate
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly making false statements of fact to clients or to OED, submitting false evidence, or otherwise misleading OED in response to RFIs constitutes a separate violation and reflects failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigations (Counts II, IV, VI, VIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include representing that a client had signed a statement when they had not, or not disclosing that a client refused to sign; failure to correct such misrepresentations aggravates sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper cessation of representation (withdrawal duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceasing representation of a client without obtaining permission from the Office or without properly notifying the client can constitute a violation (Count IX and related findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must follow the applicable rules/procedures for withdrawal; unilateral inaction leading to abandonment of client matters is not an adequate withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of attorney responsibilities and receipt of Office communications
rubrics_metrics.description: When an attorney is granted power of attorney, all USPTO communications in those applications are sent only to the attorney, and the attorney is responsible for receiving, acting on, and communicating about those Office communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to manage communications after receiving power of attorney (e.g., not forwarding Office Actions or Notices to the client) is evidence of neglect and can support sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival petition requirements for abandoned applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to revive an abandoned patent application requires a statement that the entire delay was unintentional and may require PTO inquiries; revival requires paying petition fees and may not always be possible, and revived patents may have reduced term (35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical considerations: fees for petitions (example amounts discussed), the need to make a convincing unintentionality statement, and potential substantive consequences (reduced term or inability to revive) are relevant to assessing client injury from abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment factor: extent of actual or potential injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual or potential injury to clients and to the Office resulting from the misconduct is a primary consideration in determining the appropriate sanction (e.g., financial cost to revive applications, diminished patent term, lost opportunities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision weighed greater injury (e.g., to Openiano) more heavily when computing suspension lengths; harms to clients and to OED's investigative burden are both considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors for sanction determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include substantial experience in the practice of law; dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; submission of false evidence or statements; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding; and refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific aggravators (drawn from ABA Standards and the record) justify increasing the sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors for sanction determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors may include the absence of a prior disciplinary record and other factors tending to reduce culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the absence of prior discipline was the sole mitigating factor; mitigation is balanced against aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing intent from negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of culpability (intentional misconduct versus negligence or inadvertence) affects findings and the severity of sanctions; the record should support whether failures (e.g., not informing clients) were intentional or negligent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for some clients the conduct was found intentional; for others the evidence supported negligence; intentional misconduct yields harsher sanctioning weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning methodology and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions are determined by balancing aggravating and mitigating factors, the extent of injury, and relevant precedent and ABA Standards; administrative law judges compare similar prior cases (cited precedents) when choosing suspension length and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites Moatz v. Bode, In re Kroll, Small v. Weiffenbach, In re Klein, and ABA Standards in arriving at a three-year suspension plus probation and MPRE requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinstatement to practice may be conditioned on passing the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE) and compliance with a probationary period and disciplinary rules; passing score determined by relevant state bar rules (here, California).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The respondent must demonstrate knowledge of disciplinary rules and serve probation (two years in this case) after reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of suspended practitioners and petitions for reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspended practitioners must comply with duties set out in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; petitions for reinstatement are governed by 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 and the Office’s procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's attention is directed to those regulations as part of the sanction order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure from Initial Decision (37 C.F.R. § 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any appeal from the Initial Decision must be filed with the USPTO within 30 days, and must include exceptions to the ALJ’s decision and supporting reasons; failure to file an appeal in accordance with § 11.55 is deemed acceptance of the decision and waiver of further review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness and content requirements are mandatory; the decision warns of consequences for failing to appeal properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED investigative process and RFIs (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may issue Requests for Information (RFIs) seeking documents and explanations; practitioners are required to respond, and failure to respond or to cooperate with OED's investigation can itself be the basis for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated RFIs, failure to provide requested statements, or submitting false attachments are described as factors supporting violation findings and aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and client file obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to maintain and be able to produce client files and records; inability or refusal to locate or provide client records in response to OED inquiries can be evidence of misconduct or obstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes relocation and disorganization of files as part of OED's inquiry; not searching for files when they are under one's control is unfavorable to the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner demeanor and acknowledgement of wrongdoing as sanction-relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct, lack of remorse, hostile courtroom behavior, or blaming others during proceedings can aggravate sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the record (shouting, insults, persistent denial) were discussed as particularly troubling and relevant to increasing the sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual disputes or unpaid fees do not excuse professional obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner’s claim that a client failed to pay agreed fees does not relieve the attorney of professional duties to timely respond to PTO communications, to properly withdraw, or to notify the client of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision rejects the argument that simple contract law excuses failure to act and emphasizes that procedure and client-protection obligations cannot be subordinated to fee collection.
